The AVBSPR system is based on a five-axis SCROBOT-ER VII robot with an eye-in-hand stereoscopic image capture module.
Surgical markers are composed of three IR emitters arranged in a triangle with unequal side lengths.
The system uses two CCD cameras with 640x480 resolution to capture stereoscopic images.
A targeting window of 120x160 pixels is defined within the camera images for tracking.
3D coordinates are computed by triangulating the image coordinates from the two cameras using geometric formulas.
Fuzzy logic is employed for image servo tracking to dynamically track moving surgical markers and generate motor velocity commands.
The fuzzy control model uses inputs of relative distance (in pixels) and angle (in degrees) to output motor velocity commands.
The system achieves a positioning error of approximately 5 mm within a 2000 mm operating range.
The DSP module used is the TI TMS 320C32 processor, implementing PID control, forward and inverse kinematics.
The system's sampling rate and control command frequency is approximately 30 Hz (1/30 second).
The control circuit includes a DSP-based servo motion controller, multi-axis control and communication board, and power drive modules.
The intelligent software modules are developed in Microsoft Visual C++ and integrated into a GUI.
Experimental tests show the robot can track surgical markers well with positioning errors around 5 mm.
The fuzzy logic controller is decoupled into horizontal and vertical motion models with separate rule tables.
The system prototype is intended for navigation in orthopedic surgeries.
The system can reset the robot arm to a pre-specified position and then capture stereoscopic images for tracking.
The fuzzy logic controller uses fuzzification, rule base categorization, inference engine, and defuzzification steps.
The surgical marker's triangular configuration allows unique determination of position and orientation.
The system integrates image processing, encoder feedback, and position and velocity control in a closed loop.
The paper reports that the system can dynamically track moving surgical markers and determine best image capture orientation in real-time.
